item.text: {"text":"Recent work separates factual grounding from personalized relevance. [PURE (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03080) identifies explanations that cite correct item attributes yet conflict with historical preferences; generic evidence can also be weakly personalized. [Walk the Talk? (2025)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/b5ec50eb177908f21f78ed0d76ed525c-Abstract-Conference.html) shows plausible explanations can misrepresent influential evidence. Applied here, a proposed taxonomy is: recent specific support, broad lexical overlap only, explicit specification conflict, and insufficient evidence. Record history item IDs, timestamps, exact title/description spans, and any actual feedback supporting each judgment. Historical interaction supports observed interest, not ownership, satisfaction, or a mandatory compatibility requirement; missing specifications imply unknown fit, not conflict.\n\nAbstention should be evaluated alongside coverage. [Trust or Escalate (2025)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/08dabd5345b37fffcbe335bd578b15a0-Paper-Conference.pdf) calibrates automated judgments against human agreement and escalates uncertain cases. For the twenty users, compare probe labels with their actual feedback using a fixed rubric; report per-label counts, agreement, conflict precision, and abstention coverage, with uncertainty and category breakdowns. Distinguish disagreement from feedback that never addresses the claimed attribute. [Human Feedback Is Not Gold Standard (2024)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/f719b8ca81221f380836e573d479c223-Abstract-Conference.html) finds feedback can be confounded by assertiveness and complexity, supporting neutral wording and independent annotation where feasible. These are proposed diagnostic procedures, not validated findings for these users; twenty users provide a small exploratory audit."}
